title: Projected Talking Jack-o'-Lantern - inflatable Halloween prop
oneLiner: An inflatable pumpkin with a projector inside it that throws an animated, lip-syncing jack-o'-lantern face onto a translucent panel in its skin. A kid talks to it; it answers in character.

provenance.postureMeaning: No supplier has been contacted. No quote has been received. No unit has been built. Every cost in this file is a researched BAND or a stated ESTIMATE, never a quoted price. Nothing here constitutes a manufacturing commitment.
provenance.trackRecord: none - this venture has never been produced or sold
provenance.howToUpgrade: Every record with needsQuote:true is a line where a real supplier quote replaces the band. The engine must report the share of landed cost still resting on needsQuote lines; that share is the honest confidence in the whole plan.

confidenceScale.high: Directly observed on a primary/retail surface, or computed from first principles with inputs of at least medium confidence.
confidenceScale.medium: Reported by a credible secondary source (trade guide, compliance lab, freight broker) as a market range; consistent across more than one source.
confidenceScale.low: Single source, or an inference from an adjacent category. Treat as a placeholder that a quote must replace.

softwareBaseline.note: What already exists, established by reading the code - not by asking a model. This is the only part of the venture with a real as-built status.

exists.what: Full-screen procedural jack-o'-lantern face renderer, HTML5 canvas, 60fps, at /pumpkin/
The 'inflatable' preset renders a PURE BLACK background (#000000) so only the carved features emit light; the pumpkin body colour comes from the fabric itself, not the projector
exists.evidence: BUILTIN_PRESETS.inflatable in pumpkin-engine-presets.ts: colors.background '#000000', feature '#ffb020', featureHot '#fff3c0', glow.blur 44
exists.whyItMatters: This is the single most favourable engineering fact in the venture. A mostly-black frame means a cheap low-contrast projector's black level lands below the ambient-lit fabric, so no visible rectangle. See gate TG-3.

exists.what: Lip-sync driven by real per-frame RMS of the OUTPUT audio (WebAudio AnalyserNode), not a canned mouth loop
Two conversation modes: mimic (mic -> STT -> speak back, zero LLM) and autonomous (guest speech -> pumpkin-bot -> in-character reply)
A DETERMINISTIC zero-cost in-character reply bank already exists for the public demo path
exists.evidence: demoReply() in pumpkin-app.js - keyed on trick/treat/candy, name, scary/spooky/boo, plus a rotating fallback set
exists.whyItMatters: This is the shipping answer for a retail SKU that must work with no cloud account and no per-utterance token cost. See risk R-4.

exists.what: Unattended-night hardening: self-healing SSE room link with jittered backoff, self-echo rejection, single-flight replies, a 45s think deadline, speak queue, screen Wake Lock
Swarm control door POST /api/pumpkin/speak (service-secret only) plus two manifest-declared tools

doesNotExistAndBlocksRetail.what: The projector page requires an OIDC sign-in with a HARD 24-hour absolute session cap that nothing resets. When it expires the prop shows a 'Signed out' panel and a human must walk to the device and sign in again.
doesNotExistAndBlocksRetail.whyItMatters: A consumer product cannot require a daily browser sign-in to a self-hosted identity provider. A retail SKU needs either a device-token pairing rail or a fully local offline runtime.
mitigationCandidates: Wire the existing core /api/tv/pair/* 30-day device-token rail to pumpkin (README says this is explicitly NOT built)
Ship a fully local runtime with no server dependency for the mimic + deterministic-reply modes
doesNotExistAndBlocksRetail.estimateBasis: ESTIMATE - no scoping session has been held. Range reflects device-token rail (low) vs a standalone local runtime (high).

doesNotExistAndBlocksRetail.what: Autonomous mode costs LLM tokens per utterance, charged to whoever owns the account. There is no per-unit funding model.
doesNotExistAndBlocksRetail.whyItMatters: At retail this is a recurring COGS per unit with no revenue attached. Forces one of: a subscription, an on-device small model, or shipping the deterministic reply bank (SW-5) as the default and making AI an opt-in upsell.

doesNotExistAndBlocksRetail.what: No enclosure, no mechanical design, no thermal or ingress design, no packaging, no manufacturing partner, no certification.

variants.name: Self-contained unit
variants.description: Everything in the box: inflatable envelope with a translucent projection panel, blower, short-throw projector, compute module running the face locally, speaker, mic, power distribution, stakes. Plug into one outdoor GFCI outlet and it works.
variants.strategicNote: Its landed cost pushes retail to roughly 3x the dominant inflatable price anchor, so it cannot be merchandised as an inflatable. It must be merchandised as an animatronic, where the observed shelf band is 169 to 399 USD.

variants.name: BYO-device kit
variants.description: Inflatable envelope with translucent projection panel, blower, stakes, an internal universal projector cradle, and a printed card with a QR to the software. The customer supplies their own projector (or phone plus a cheap projector) and their own network.
variants.strategicNote: Lands near the observed inflatable price anchor with the software as the differentiator. The customer absorbs the single largest BOM line. This may be the real business; the engine should be able to reach that conclusion from the numbers rather than being told it.

variants.name: Software only
variants.description: No hardware at all. A seasonal licence to the face renderer, presets and voice, for a customer who already owns a projector and a screen or an inflatable.
variants.strategicNote: Near-zero COGS, no tariff exposure, no certification, no inventory, no seasonal working capital. The observed comparable digital-decoration download price is 24.99 USD. It is the only tier that can ship this season.

bom.spec: 6 ft tall pumpkin body, 210D or heavier polyester oxford, coated, sewn seams, printed orange with carved-relief detail; integrated sleeve for the translucent face panel
bom.note: Bracketed against observed finished retail: a plain 8 ft inflatable retails 27 to 70 USD (S7, S28), implying a landed cost well under 20 USD for a simpler envelope. This spec is smaller but adds a panel sleeve and a rigid internal mount.

bom.spec: Purpose-made diffusing panel, 18 to 35 percent transmittance, welded or sewn into the envelope front, tensioned so blower pressure does not ripple the image
bom.note: NOT optional and NOT the same fabric as the envelope. Standard coated 210D oxford is far too opaque to rear-project through. Getting this wrong makes the whole product dark.

bom.spec: 120 V outdoor-rated cold-air blower, 100 to 400 CFM, integrated cord and GFCI-compatible plug
150 to 400 ANSI lumens (measured, with test report), 720p minimum, throw ratio 0.5 to 0.8, HDMI in, LED light engine with 20000 h rated life, keystone correction
bom.note: Wholesale tiers observed: entry 7-15 USD, mid-range smart 1080p 25-95 USD, DLP pocket 120-185 USD (S2); DLP OEM modules 85-420 USD (S1). The 28-85 band assumes the mid-range LCD class. THE BAND IS UNSAFE UNTIL A SUPPLIER CONFIRMS SHORT THROW IS AVAILABLE IN IT - the cheap class is built around 1.2-1.5:1. If short throw is only available in the DLP module tier, this line triples and the V-A business case likely fails. See gate TG-1 and risk R-1.

bom.spec: ARM SBC or Android stick class, HDMI out, 802.11ac WiFi, capable of a hardware-composited kiosk browser at 60fps, MIC input or USB audio
bom.note: Low end is the OEM Android TV stick class; high end is a Raspberry Pi CM5 (published 45 to 95 USD retail single-unit, S23) which buys long-term supply and a real Linux. The choice is a supply-security vs cost tradeoff, not just a price tradeoff.

bom.spec: 10 W class D amp, weather-tolerant full-range driver, mounted at the base firing out through a mesh port
bom.note: Mounting matters more than the driver: a driver inside the fabric bag is muffled and coloured by the envelope. Base-mounted with an external port.

bom.spec: Far-field MEMS mic or 2-mic array with basic noise rejection, mounted at the base facing the walkway
bom.note: Outdoor far-field speech capture at 6 to 10 ft over blower noise is a genuinely hard audio problem. The blower is a continuous broadband noise source located INSIDE the same enclosure. See risk R-5.

bom.spec: Single-inlet IEC or moulded cord, internal fusing, 12 V and 5 V rails, strain relief, the assembly that a UL/ETL listing actually evaluates
bom.note: This is the component the safety listing is really about. Cheapening it is where a certification failure comes from.

bom.spec: IP44 minimum rigid housing with a sealed optical window, unobstructed intake and exhaust paths, and a cage that keeps fabric off the exhaust

bom.note: The blower pulls OUTDOOR air in continuously - humid, sometimes rain-laden. Condensation on a cold optical surface is the realistic overnight failure. See risk R-3.

technicalGates.question: Does the projector geometry close inside the envelope?
technicalGates.formula: throwDistanceIn = throwRatio * imageWidthIn; PASS if throwDistanceIn <= usableInternalPathIn

workedCases.case: cheap 1.2:1 projector, 28 in face, 34 in horizontal path
workedCases.verdict: FAIL - 0.4 in of margin is not a design margin, it is a coincidence

workedCases.case: cheap 1.5:1 projector, 28 in face, 34 in horizontal path
short-throw 0.8:1, 28 in face, 34 in horizontal path
short-throw 0.5:1, 28 in face, 34 in horizontal path
cheap 1.5:1 firing UP the long axis to an angled panel, 28 in face, 60 in path
workedCases.verdict: PASS - but introduces a keystone/focus-plane problem

technicalGates.verdict: CONDITIONAL PASS. A standard 1.2-1.5:1 mini projector does NOT close across the width of a 6 ft envelope at a 28 in face. Two ways out: buy a short-throw lens (unproven at this price point - A-GEO-3 needsQuote) or fire up the long axis and correct keystone (free in BOM, costs mechanical design). The incumbent's existence at 99.99 USD retail (C-1) is evidence the long-axis approach works.
technicalGates.resolveBy: Ask three mini-projector suppliers for a 0.5-0.8 throw ratio unit at 5000 pcs with a measured ANSI lumens test report. If none exists under 90 USD, commit to the long-axis geometry and prototype the keystone quality.

technicalGates.question: Is the projected face actually visible in an outdoor yard?
technicalGates.formula: E_full_lux = ansiLumens / imageArea_m2; featureLuminance_nits = E_full_lux * panelTransmittance / PI; ambientFabricLuminance_nits = ambientLux * fabricReflectance / PI; contrastRatio = featureLuminance / ambientFabricLuminance

workedCases.case: 150 ANSI (low band), tau 0.18 (low band), full dark (5 lux)
workedCases.verdict: PASS - worst-case corner still clearly visible

workedCases.case: 250 ANSI, tau 0.25, one hour before sunset (1000 lux)

technicalGates.verdict: PASS after dark, FAIL before dark. The worst-case corner of the input bands still gives 32:1 contrast in a dark yard, so this is robust rather than marginal. Failing in daylight is normal for the whole category and is not a defect - but the packaging and listing copy must say 'after dark' plainly, because a customer who unboxes it at 4pm on Halloween and sees nothing will return it.
technicalGates.resolveBy: Nothing. This gate is closed by arithmetic on researched bands. Confirm with a measured panel transmittance once a sample exists.

technicalGates.question: Does a cheap projector's poor black level show a visible glowing rectangle on the pumpkin?
technicalGates.formula: blackIllum_lux = E_full_lux / contrastRatio; blackLuminance_nits = blackIllum_lux * panelTransmittance / PI; INVISIBLE if blackLuminance_nits < ambientFabricLuminance_nits

workedCases.verdict: INVISIBLE - projected black is 11x DIMMER than the ambient-lit fabric around it

workedCases.case: 250 ANSI, contrast 200:1 (worst band), tau 0.25, 5 lux ambient
workedCases.verdict: INVISIBLE - still below the ambient-lit fabric

workedCases.case: 250 ANSI, contrast 200:1, tau 0.25, 1 lux ambient (very dark rural yard)
workedCases.verdict: FAINTLY VISIBLE - a dim rectangle in a very dark yard at the worst contrast corner

technicalGates.verdict: PASS, and this is a case where doing the arithmetic overturned the intuition. The obvious fear - that a cheap projector paints a grey box on the pumpkin - is wrong in a typical suburban yard because the shipped preset renders a PURE BLACK background (SW-2), so the black field is at 0.07 to 0.30 nits against fabric that ambient light already raises to 0.80 nits. Only at the worst contrast corner in a very dark rural yard does a faint rectangle appear, and a projected soft-edge vignette in the renderer removes even that.
technicalGates.resolveBy: Specify contrast >= 400:1 measured on/off in the projector quote, and add a soft-edged vignette to the 'inflatable' preset. Both are cheap.
technicalGates.engineeringActionForSoftware: Add a radial soft-edge vignette to the inflatable preset so the frame boundary is never a hard edge. This is a small change to the existing renderer, not new work.

technicalGates.question: Does a projector running for six hours cook the inside of the inflatable?
technicalGates.formula: heat_BTUhr = projectorWatts * heatFraction * 3.412; deltaT_F = heat_BTUhr / (1.08 * CFM)

workedCases.case: 60 W projector (high band), 100 CFM blower (low band)
60 W projector, 50 CFM effective through the projector zone

technicalGates.verdict: PASS. A cold-air inflatable is not sealed - the blower runs continuously and the fabric leaks by design (A-THM-3), so the interior is a moving air stream, not an oven. Even a pessimistic 50 CFM through the projector zone gives under 4 degF of bulk rise. The residual risk is LOCAL and mechanical, not thermodynamic: fabric collapsing onto the projector's intake or exhaust when the blower cycles or the prop is knocked. B-09's cage exists for exactly that.
technicalGates.resolveBy: Nothing thermodynamic. Validate the mechanical case with a six-hour soak test on the first prototype, instrumented at the projector exhaust, with the fabric deliberately pushed against the housing.

technicalGates.question: Does weather and moisture kill it overnight?
technicalGates.verdict: OPEN AND UNRESOLVED. The same continuous airflow that solves the thermal gate is the moisture problem: the blower pulls outdoor air, including humidity, dew and blown rain, straight past the optics for six hours. A warm lens in cold humid air fogs; a cooling lens after shutdown condenses. This is the most likely source of field failures and returns and no arithmetic in this file resolves it.
technicalGates.resolveBy: Prototype an overnight dew-cycle test. Design candidates: sealed optical window with the projector's own cooling loop kept separate from the envelope air, a hydrophobic window coating, a small resistive window heater, and an orientation that keeps the window facing down-and-forward so condensate runs off.

technicalGates.question: Is one 25 ft cord to one household outlet enough?
technicalGates.formula: totalW = blowerW + projectorW + computeW + ampW; currentA = totalW / 120; vDrop = 2 * cordFt * currentA * ohmPerFt

workedCases.case: blower 120 W + projector 45 W + compute 8 W + amp 12 W, 25 ft 16 AWG
worst case: blower 180 W + projector 60 W + compute 12 W + amp 15 W

technicalGates.verdict: PASS with wide margin. One 16 AWG outdoor cord on one GFCI outlet. The real constraint is not electrical, it is that the product must present a SINGLE cord to the customer - which means an internal power distribution board (B-08), which is the assembly the safety listing evaluates.

technicalGates.question: Can it hear a child over the blower, outdoors?
technicalGates.verdict: OPEN. The blower is a continuous broadband noise source located inside the same enclosure as the microphone, roughly 2 to 4 ft away, running the entire time the prop is up. The software already handles the OTHER hard audio problem well - it hard-stops the mic before its own speech, holds a 900 ms reverb window and rejects self-echo by word overlap (SW-6) - but nothing addresses blower noise, and no measurement exists.
technicalGates.resolveBy: Measure SPL at the intended mic position with the blower running. If SNR is inadequate, the fixes are ordered by cost: mic placement outside the envelope on the base, a directional or beamforming array, a push-to-talk button on the prop, or dropping open-mic and shipping the phone remote (SW-4) as the only input path.

technicalGates.question: How does the picture get to the projector - and is streaming the right answer?
technicalGates.formula: qualitative - the operator asked for 'a way to stream to the projector'

options.approach: Compute INSIDE the prop (B-05) running a kiosk browser, HDMI to the projector. Network only for the LLM and TTS, not for the pixels.
options.why: Rendering is local, so a WiFi hiccup does not drop the face - it only degrades autonomous replies to the deterministic bank (SW-5). This is the only option that survives six unattended hours.

options.approach: Cast or mirror from a phone (Chromecast / AirPlay / Miracast).
options.why: Screen mirroring drops, the phone must stay awake and unused for six hours, battery dies, a notification overlays the face, and mirroring latency breaks the audio-driven lip-sync (SW-3) that is the product's whole trick. This is the seductive-sounding option and it is the wrong one.

options.approach: Long HDMI or HDMI-over-Cat6 from a laptop in the house.
options.why: Cheap and reliable, but it ties up a laptop and runs a cable across a yard people walk through. Acceptable for an enthusiast, not for a retail SKU.

technicalGates.verdict: The operator's word 'stream' should be read as 'get the picture there', and the correct answer is NOT to stream pixels at all - it is to move the renderer inside the prop and stream only the small amount of text and audio that autonomous mode needs. That decision drives B-05 into the BOM and is the main reason V-A costs what it costs.

regulatory.basis: The unit contains a compute module with WiFi (intentional radiator, Part 15C) and digital circuitry (unintentional radiator, Part 15B). V-B and V-C contain no radio and no digital circuitry of their own.
regulatory.costNote: Published ranges: 600-5000 USD for a non-wireless unintentional radiator; 1000-4000 USD for Bluetooth; 6500-12000 USD for WiFi-integrated (S8, S9). A WiFi module that is ALREADY FCC-certified as a module can be used under its existing grant, collapsing this to the Part 15B host test only.
regulatory.costDownLever: Buy a pre-certified WiFi module with a modular grant. This is the single biggest certification cost-down available and it is a sourcing decision, not a compliance decision.

regulatory.regime: UL or ETL listing (NRTL safety listing)
regulatory.applies: V-A and V-B (both contain a mains-powered blower)
regulatory.basis: A mains-connected consumer product sold at US retail. Major retailers stock both UL and ETL; ETL typically costs 20-30 percent less and is 20-30 percent faster.
regulatory.costNote: Published: Type L (complete stand-alone consumer product) 5000-50000 USD; ETL 20-30 percent less (S13, S14). A design that uses an ALREADY-LISTED blower and an already-listed external power supply, with the only new assembly being a low-voltage harness, sits at the bottom of this range.
regulatory.costDownLever: Use a pre-listed blower and a pre-listed external PSU. Keep every mains-voltage node inside already-listed components so the new assembly is low-voltage only.
regulatory.recurringCost: Listings carry annual factory follow-up inspection fees that the engine must model as an ongoing cost, not a one-time cost.

regulatory.applies: CONDITIONAL - and the condition is a marketing decision, not an engineering one
regulatory.basis: 16 CFR 1200.2. CPSC's stated position is that most holiday and seasonal decorations are NOT children's products even though they appeal to children. But the determination is a four-factor test: (1) the manufacturer's stated intended use, (2) how it is represented in packaging, promotion and advertising, (3) whether consumers commonly recognise it as for children 12 and under, (4) the Age Determination Guidelines.
regulatory.theTrap: This product's core selling proposition is 'a kid talks to it and it answers'. Writing that on the box is factor (2) and arguably factor (1). The marketing copy is what decides whether CPSIA applies - and therefore whether the venture takes on third-party lab testing, a Children's Product Certificate, permanent tracking labels, and component-level lead and phthalate testing on every material.
regulatory.costNote: Lab testing for a standard toy CPC covering ASTM F963 and CPSIA lead and phthalates: 380-500 USD depending on test-item count; other labs quote 500-1200 USD (S10). Per-material and per-production-lot, not once.
regulatory.mitigation: Market it as a YARD DECORATION for the homeowner, not a toy for the child. Label it as an adult-assembled decoration, do not depict a child operating it on the packaging, do not place it in a toy aisle. That keeps it in the 'seasonal decoration' interpretation. This is a deliberate, reversible marketing constraint with a real dollar value attached - the engine should price both branches.
regulatory.engineMustModel: Two scenarios: NOT-a-children's-product (no CPC cost, no tracking label, marketing copy constrained) and IS-a-children's-product (CPC testing per lot, tracking labels, ASTM F963 mechanical and flammability testing, marketing copy unconstrained).

regulatory.regime: CBP eFiling of certificates of compliance
regulatory.basis: Beginning 8 July 2026, importers of most regulated consumer products must electronically file certificates of compliance with CBP via the PGA Message Set.
regulatory.costNote: ESTIMATE - broker setup and per-entry handling. Mostly a process cost, not a fee.
regulatory.note: This is live NOW, ahead of any plausible first shipment. It is a customs-broker capability requirement, not an optional nicety.

regulatory.basis: Any product sold into California containing listed substances. Relevant candidates: phthalates in PVC or coated fabric, lead in solder and wire insulation, BPA in plastics.
regulatory.costNote: ESTIMATE - substance testing plus label design. Many importers default to a warning label as insurance, which costs nothing but can suppress conversion.

regulatory.basis: Separate from and additive to all federal requirements. Typically includes: a supplier agreement, EDI capability, GS1 UPC/GTIN, insurance certificates naming the retailer, a social-compliance factory audit, packaging and drop-test (ISTA) conformance, carton marking and pallet patterns, and a chargeback schedule for every deviation.
regulatory.costNote: ESTIMATE for a first-time vendor's setup year including EDI, audit, insurance and testing. No retailer has quoted this venture.
regulatory.note: This is the category of cost first-time vendors most reliably omit. It is not a tax on the product; it is the cost of being allowed to sell to the account at all, and it is largely incurred BEFORE the first PO.

channels.name: Direct to consumer (own storefront)

customerAcquisitionCost.note: For a seasonal product with a 6-week purchase window and no brand, paid acquisition is the whole game and CAC is the number most likely to sink the model. This band is an ESTIMATE with no campaign data behind it.

channels.calendarConstraint: Traffic must be bought in the late-August-to-September window (A-CAL-3). Outside it, near-zero intent.

channels.name: Amazon FBA
channels.theSeasonalTrap: A bulky seasonal item pays the 2.5x Q4 storage rate (1.20 vs 0.48 USD/cu ft/month) during exactly the months it is sitting in the warehouse waiting for October. And inventory that does not clear by 1 November sits at the peak rate through December for a product nobody wants until next August. The engine must charge storage on PEAK inventory in Q4, not on average inventory across the year - averaging hides the entire problem.
channels.referenceDataPoint: A 30 USD bulky home item can lose roughly 47 percent of revenue to fees before storage or advertising (S18). That is a warning about the V-B price point specifically.
channels.calendarConstraint: Inventory must be received at FBA by early September; Q4 inbound restrictions and receiving delays are real and the deadline is not negotiable.

channels.name: Big-box seasonal (Home Depot, Lowe's, Walmart, Target)
channels.calendarConstraint: Category review windows sit roughly 9 to 12 months ahead of the selling season (A-CAL-2) and outreach must start 3 to 4 months before the window (A-CAL-1). Compounded, first contact for a Halloween 2028 set happens around Q3 2027. THIS IS THE SCHEDULE DRIVER FOR THE ENTIRE VENTURE.
channels.firstTimeVendorReality: A first-time vendor with no listing, no certification, no factory audit and no production history is not a candidate for a category review. The realistic sequence is: prove sell-through in CH-1/CH-2 for one season, then pitch with data.

examples: Haunted Living 3 ft Animated LED Skeleton 169.99

observedPricePoints.note: Walmart 8 ft stacked-pumpkin inflatable observed at 40 USD marked down from 100; Home Depot Joyfy 8 ft at 69.99.

channels.name: Seasonal specialty (Spirit Halloween and similar pop-ups)
channels.note: Spirit sources heavily through OEM bases in Asia and places early orders on projections with flexible scale-up terms. That is a fit for a manufacturer, not for a first-time brand. Their public-facing vendor pages are oriented to consignment store operators, not product vendors - reaching a buyer requires a different door than the website.

channels.name: Digital download / app store

feeModel.note: ESTIMATE, standard app-store and digital-marketplace rates

channels.note: Zero COGS, zero tariff, zero certification, zero inventory, zero seasonal working capital, and it can ship THIS season. The observed comparable is the AtmosFX digital decoration download at 24.99 USD (S6). It is the only tier whose schedule is not governed by A-CAL-2.

competitors.name: Gemmy
competitors.product: Projection Airblown Inflatable, Fire and Ice Frightening Pumpkin Giant Scene, 12 ft
competitors.whatItDoes: An internally-lit inflatable with a rotating kaleidoscope LED projection unit throwing swirling colour onto the skin. Also sold as a standalone Fire and Ice projection spotlight accessory.
competitors.whatItDoesNot: It projects a colour pattern, not a rendered face. It does not lip-sync, does not listen, does not speak, and does not respond.
competitors.structuralNote: The gap is not a feature Gemmy has declined to add - it is a different product architecture. A rotating gobo has no frame buffer, no audio pipeline and no compute, so no amount of iteration on that light unit produces a face that talks. Closing the gap means adding a video engine, a renderer, an audio path and a network stack - which is the BOM difference between their 99.99 USD unit and this venture's V-A.
competitors.whatItProvesForUs: This is the most valuable competitive fact in the file, and it is good news. It establishes that a projector inside a cold-air inflatable, outdoors, for a full Halloween season, at a 99.99 USD RETAIL price, is a solved manufacturing problem. The geometry, the thermal behaviour, the weather tolerance and the retail acceptance are all demonstrated by a shipping product. This venture is not inventing the physical form factor - it is putting a different light engine inside a proven one.
competitors.whatItCostsUs: It also sets the price anchor on the inflatables shelf at 99.99 USD. V-A cannot be merchandised there.

competitors.name: AtmosFX (and licensed kit assemblers such as HoliScapes)
competitors.product: Digital decoration content plus projector-and-screen kits, including Jack-O-Lantern Jamboree

priceComparisonPoints.what: HoliScapes USB projector kit with Jack-O-Lantern Jamboree, 720p LED projector, remote, wide-angle lens, 48x72 in translucent screen - marketplace listing
The SAME kit at a mass retailer
The same kit at a home-improvement retailer
AtmosFX Jack-O-Lantern Jamboree digital decoration, content only

competitors.whatItDoes: Pre-rendered video loops projected onto a flat translucent screen in a window or doorway. Very high production quality.
competitors.whatItDoesNot: The content is pre-rendered video. It cannot respond to a specific child, cannot say a name, cannot answer a question, and its mouth is not driven by anything that is happening in the yard.
competitors.structuralNote: A pre-rendered library and a real-time procedural renderer are different things. A video file cannot lip-sync to a sentence that did not exist when the file was made; the shipped renderer here drives the mouth from the live RMS of the audio it is speaking (SW-3). That difference is architectural, not a matter of adding more loops to the library.
competitors.whatItProvesForUs: It brackets what a projector-plus-screen Halloween bundle sells for direct, at 229.99-414.99 USD depending on the surface - a band that straddles the V-A target rather than sitting above it - and it validates a 24.99 USD price for content alone, which is the V-C comparable.
competitors.whatItCostsUs: It sets a very high production-quality bar for the visuals. A procedural face has to look deliberately stylised and good, not like a cheaper version of rendered video.
competitors.priceDispersionNote: The identical kit sells at 229.99 USD at a mass retailer and 414.99 USD on a marketplace listing - a 1.8x spread on the same box. Recording only the higher surface is how a comparable becomes an argument. The verdict of this plan turns on this number, so both ends are modelled and the low end is the one to plan against: it is the price a customer comparing the two would pay.

competitors.name: The animatronics shelf generally
competitors.product: Motion- and sound-activated animated props (skeletons, dolls, groundbreakers)
competitors.whatItDoes: Triggered by a motion sensor, plays one of a small set of canned audio lines with a servo-driven motion sequence.
competitors.whatItDoesNot: It plays back; it does not converse. The line it says is unrelated to anything the visitor said.
competitors.structuralNote: This is the shelf V-A must be merchandised on and the price band it must land in. The differentiation claim that survives scrutiny is narrow and true: the props on this shelf respond to PRESENCE, this one can respond to WORDS. State it that way and it is defensible.

criticalRisks.title: Short-throw optics may not exist at the assumed price
criticalRisks.impact: If a 0.5-0.8 throw ratio is only available in the 120-420 USD DLP module tier, the V-A BOM rises by roughly 70 to 340 USD per unit and the V-A business case very likely fails.
criticalRisks.mitigation: Fire up the long axis and correct keystone (A-GEO-5), which costs mechanical design instead of BOM.
criticalRisks.resolveBy: Three supplier quotes with measured ANSI lumens and stated throw ratio.

criticalRisks.title: Tariff classification is unresolved and the swing exceeds the margin
criticalRisks.impact: Roughly 22 percentage points of landed cost between the 9505-festive and 8528-projector classifications - larger than the projected net margin in most scenarios.
criticalRisks.mitigation: None available by design choice; it is a legal classification question.
criticalRisks.resolveBy: A CBP binding ruling request, or a customs broker's written classification opinion, BEFORE any purchase order.

criticalRisks.title: Moisture and condensation on the optics
criticalRisks.impact: The most likely field-failure and returns driver. It fails at night, unattended, which is the worst possible failure mode for the customer experience.
criticalRisks.mitigation: Sealed optical window, separated cooling path, hydrophobic coating, window heater, downward-facing orientation.

criticalRisks.title: The AI is a per-unit recurring cost with no revenue attached
criticalRisks.impact: Every autonomous utterance costs LLM and TTS tokens charged to someone. At retail there is no account, no subscription and no billing relationship.
criticalRisks.mitigation: Ship the deterministic reply bank that ALREADY EXISTS (SW-5) as the retail default, and make cloud AI an opt-in upsell for owners who connect an account. This turns a recurring COGS into optional recurring revenue.
criticalRisks.resolveBy: A product decision, plus wiring the existing demoReply path as the default for an unpaired unit.

criticalRisks.title: Far-field speech capture over blower noise is unmeasured
criticalRisks.impact: If the prop cannot hear a child from the walkway, the headline feature does not work and the product is an expensive light.
criticalRisks.mitigation: Ordered by cost: mic placement, directional array, push-to-talk on the prop, or ship the existing phone remote (SW-4) as the only input.
criticalRisks.resolveBy: SPL measurement at the mic position with the blower running.

criticalRisks.title: The software cannot run unattended without a daily sign-in
criticalRisks.impact: A 24-hour hard session cap means the prop dies mid-party and needs a human at the device. Unacceptable in a retail product.
criticalRisks.mitigation: Wire the device-token pairing rail, or ship a fully local runtime.
criticalRisks.resolveBy: A scoping session; estimated 3 to 8 weeks, ESTIMATE with low confidence.

criticalRisks.title: The children's-product determination is decided by marketing copy
criticalRisks.impact: Writing the product's most compelling selling line on the box may pull it into CPSIA scope, adding per-lot lab testing, a Children's Product Certificate and permanent tracking labels.
criticalRisks.mitigation: Position as a yard decoration for the homeowner; do not depict a child operating it; stay out of the toy aisle.
criticalRisks.resolveBy: A compliance opinion on the intended packaging copy BEFORE the packaging is printed.

criticalRisks.title: Seasonal working-capital trough
criticalRisks.impact: The factory is paid in full at bill of lading, months before the season; the retailer pays 60 to 90 days after it. Peak cash need lands before any revenue arrives, and unsold inventory has near-zero residual value after 1 November.
criticalRisks.mitigation: Smaller first run, DTC-first to collect cash at the point of sale, and a returns/markdown reserve modelled explicitly.
criticalRisks.resolveBy: The engine must produce a monthly cash-flow trough figure, not just an annual P&L. An annual P&L on a seasonal product hides the only number that can kill the company.

criticalRisks.title: The category-review calendar puts a big-box shelf two seasons out
criticalRisks.impact: For a product that does not yet exist, the earliest realistic big-box shelf date is two Halloweens away. Any plan that assumes a big-box launch next season is wrong.
criticalRisks.mitigation: Sequence the channels: V-C ships this season at near-zero cost, V-B/DTC next season builds sell-through data, big-box the season after with that data in hand.

goldenVectors.purpose: Hand-derived expected values for the engine's deterministic calculators. These are regression guards: they assert the engine's ARITHMETIC, computed independently of the engine. Any engine change that moves these numbers without a corresponding assumption change is a bug.

vectors.note: V-A at 5000 units, excluding tooling amortisation and the optional remote B-15. Hand-verified against the bom array on 2026-08-01.
vectors.rationale: The band is 2.85x wide from low to high. An engine that collapses this to a point estimate has destroyed the only honest thing about it.

vectors.note: V-B at 5000 units, excluding tooling. Asserts LINE SELECTION, which is what a variant-filter bug breaks.
Tariff classification scenario spread on the V-A midpoint - the engine must return BOTH branches, never one.
vectors.rationale: 29.05 USD of unresolved duty on a unit whose entire target net margin is smaller than that. This single number is why A-DUT-3 is ranked second in openQuestionsRankedByLeverage.

vectors.note: The honesty guard. Asserts the engine can report what share of landed cost rests on lines that have never been quoted.
vectors.rationale: For V-A every single BOM line is needsQuote:true except B-14. If the engine ever reports a needsQuote share near zero it has lost the provenance, and a plan that has lost its provenance is exactly the hallucinated bill of materials this whole architecture exists to prevent.

sanityExpectations.purpose: An INDEPENDENT hand-check, computed outside the engine on 2026-08-01, recorded so a human can tell whether the engine is working and so this finding is not lost. These are NOT engine outputs and must never be presented as the plan's conclusions - the engine recomputes them from the assumptions above and its numbers are the authority. If the engine disagrees with these by more than a few percent, one of the two is broken and that must be resolved before any output is trusted.
sanityExpectations.method: landed = exWorks + freight + duty + broker, where freight = (lclRate + cfsHandling) * (1 + surcharge) * boxedCBM. Required retail through big-box = landed / (1 - vendorGrossMargin 0.40) / (1 - retailerGrossMargin 0.45). Required retail through DTC = landed / (1 - 0.38 for payment fees, CAC and returns reserve combined).

checks.scenario: V-A midpoint, 25 percent duty, peak-season freight
V-A midpoint, 7.5 percent duty, peak-season freight
V-A simultaneous LOW corner of every band, 7.5 percent duty, low freight
V-A simultaneous HIGH corner, 25 percent duty, peak freight
V-B midpoint, 25 percent duty, peak freight
V-B simultaneous LOW corner, 7.5 percent duty, low freight

whatTheArithmeticSays: V-A CANNOT reach a big-box shelf. At midpoint it needs 578 to 666 USD of retail price against an observed animatronics ceiling of 399.99 USD - it misses by 45 to 67 percent. It fits only if every single band lands at its low corner simultaneously (303.91 USD), and hitting thirteen low corners at once is not a plan, it is a wish.
V-A DOES work direct-to-consumer at roughly 349 USD, where the midpoint requirement is 308 to 355 USD. That is a real, defensible premium product - it just is not a retail-shelf product.

V-B cannot reach a big-box shelf either. At midpoint it needs 232 USD against a 69.99 USD inflatables ceiling and a 99.99 USD incumbent anchor. At its low corner it needs 125 USD, still above the anchor.

V-B works direct-to-consumer at 99 to 129 USD ONLY near the low corner (66 USD required) and is marginal at midpoint (123 USD required). The swing factor is customer acquisition cost, which has no data behind it at all.

V-C is the only tier with no COGS, no tariff exposure, no certification, no inventory, no seasonal cash trough and no dependence on the 9-to-12-month category-review calendar. It is the only tier that can ship this season.
sanityExpectations.impliedSequence: V-C this season to establish demand and buy CAC data at near-zero risk; V-B direct next season if the CAC data supports it; V-A as a premium DTC product, not a shelf product. Big-box is not reachable at any BOM corner that is not the simultaneous best case, and the category-review calendar (A-CAL-2) puts it two seasons out regardless. The engine should reach this conclusion from the numbers - it must not be told it.
sanityExpectations.confidence: The DIRECTION of these conclusions is robust: the gaps are 45 to 230 percent, far larger than the uncertainty in any single band. The absolute figures are not robust - 99.7 percent of the V-A ex-works cost sits on lines that have never been quoted.

engineRequirements.note: What the calculators must do for this dataset to be usable. Stated as requirements on the engine, not as results.
mustCompute: BOM roll-up per variant at a stated quantity, carrying low/mid/high through every line rather than collapsing to a point estimate
Tooling amortisation over the run volume as a separate visible line
Landed cost = ex-works + freight (with the peak-season surcharge branch) + duty (BOTH classification scenarios) + broker and inbound
Margin waterfall from retail price down through channel fees, retailer margin, programme allowances, returns reserve, landed cost
Volume/price curve and break-even units per variant per channel
MONTHLY cash flow with an explicit peak-trough figure - an annual P&L on a seasonal product hides the number that kills the company
Working capital timing from supplier deposit through bill-of-lading payment, transit, warehouse dwell, sell-through and retailer payment terms
Headcount cost from a role list times a labour-rate assumption the operator supplies
Certification cost and lead time rolled onto the critical path, since A-CAL-2 makes schedule the binding constraint, not cost
mustNeverDo: Present a single landed cost while A-DUT-3 is UNRESOLVED
Average Q4 storage across the year (A-CH-4)
Multiply feature luminance by the duty cycle (A-OPT-4 modelingNote)
Report a total that hides how much of it rests on needsQuote lines (GV-11)
Accept a vendor 'lumens' figure that is not stated as measured ANSI lumens (A-OPT-1 dataQualityWarning)
